name: Poem of Gilgameš (eBL Corpus text L I.4), the online critical edition of the Epic of Gilgamesh in the electronic Babylonian Library at LMU Munich
date: The Standard Babylonian chapters (Tablets I to XII) carry a publication timestamp of 13 October 2022 in the eBL API. The eBL annual report for 2022 says the Corpus was 'greatly enlarged' that year, chiefly with Gilgamesh. The platform went public in February 2023. The edition is continuously revised: the database records bibliography merges as recent as August 2026, and the parser version differs between chapters (6.1.0 and 6.2.0), which shows chapters being re-processed after first publication. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/XI ; https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://phys.org/news/2023-02-ai-texts-thousands-years-readable.html
creator: Edited by Andrew R. George (SOAS, author of the 2003 Oxford critical edition), with revision by Geraldina Rozzi and Enrique Jiménez of the eBL team at LMU Munich. English translation by George. Arabic translation of Tablets I to III by Anmar A. Fadhil (University of Baghdad) and a second translator recorded as Khatabe. Standard citation form: George, A. R. (2022), Poem of Gilgameš Chapter Standard Babylonian I, with contributions by E. Jiménez and G. Rozzi, electronic Babylonian Library, https://doi.org/10.5282/ebl/l/1/4. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/I ; https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091
form: Online critical edition and dataset. Each line is given as a normalised Akkadian reconstruction (marked for metrical feet and caesura), then a score: the line exactly as it survives on every manuscript that preserves it, stacked one under the other, with breaks shown in square brackets. Translation, notes, parallels to other chapters and colophons sit alongside. Every word is lemmatised and linked to the dictionary, and every manuscript to its museum number, photographs and bibliography. The whole thing is also exposed as JSON through a public API. It covers 39 chapters: Standard Babylonian I to XII, 14 Old Babylonian tablets (including the Schøyen and Penn pieces), 11 Middle Babylonian ones from Nippur, Ur, Hattusa, Emar, Megiddo and Ugarit, and two Neo-Assyrian outliers. The text record gives about 3,150 verses. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4 ; https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/
effect_on_arc: The edition's biggest effect is on what counts as 'the text'. George's 2003 volumes fixed the poem at one moment. The eBL version keeps absorbing finds made since, including the Sulaymaniyah Tablet V material (al-Rawi and George 2014) and the Babylon-collection fragments Jiménez published in 2020. The site's own introduction says it 'incorporates all discoveries since then, both large and small.' The clearest change to a character sits in Tablet XI, line 74. Before the flood, Utnapishtim now says 'I lavished on my workforce like the waters of a river'. The reading rests on a new fragment, and the note openly lists rival restorations, one of them suggested by George himself. Foster reads the lavishness as guilt towards men who will drown, which makes the flood hero more troubled than the older text allowed. The edition also makes the poem's circularity easy to check: the note to XI 324 points out that the epic closes by repeating the prologue's description of Uruk's walls, and the score cross-links the two passages line by line. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4 ; https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/XI ; https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/12/books/booksupdate/ai-ancient-tablets-gilgamesh.html
critical_response: Almost all published comment comes from the project itself or from press coverage of the Fragmentarium: Jiménez in The Conversation (2023), LMU press releases, and the New York Times (Erik Ofgang, August 2024). Scholars now cite the eBL chapters by DOI next to George 2003, which shows the edition has been accepted as a standard reference. The IAA 'In the Spotlight' profile describes the aim as giving 'every reader, specialist or not, ... immediate access to the current state of scholarship.' I found no independent scholarly review of the Gilgamesh edition as an edition [uncertain]. Sources: https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091 ; https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/12/books/booksupdate/ai-ancient-tablets-gilgamesh.html
controversies: No public dispute over the Gilgamesh edition itself. The method raises two quieter questions. The first is editorial. eBL prints a normalised text in Standard Babylonian grammar, and the project says this 'somewhat departs from the Assyriological tradition of editing "eclectic" texts' that combine readings from several manuscripts. Some philologists prefer a text that stays closer to what a single scribe wrote. The second is stability. A living edition can change after you cite it, and eBL keeps no obvious public version history for individual lines. That makes the DOI point to a moving target, whereas a page reference in George 2003 stays fixed. Both points are my reading of the design rather than published critiques [uncertain]. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/about/corpus ; https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4
regional_reception: Arabic sits in the edition itself: Tablets I to III have line-by-line Arabic translations beside George's English, credited to Anmar A. Fadhil of the University of Baghdad and to Khatabe. That is rare for a critical edition of Gilgamesh and means the poem can be read in Arabic in the country where the tablets were written. The later tablets are English only so far. The Iraq Museum is a formal eBL partner, and the edition includes Iraq Museum manuscripts such as IM 67564 from Kalhu (Nimrud) in Tablet XI. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/I ; https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/XI ; https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/
method: Traditional cuneiform scholarship, set in a database. George's 2003 score was converted into eBL's structured ATF format, and Rozzi and Jiménez then revised it against new joins and newly identified fragments. Every manuscript line is aligned word by word to the reconstructed line, so a reader can see which tablet supplies which word. The edition is tied to the eBL Fragmentarium: its string-alignment search compares every transliterated fragment against the Corpus, and a new hit shows up as a new manuscript or join in the score (for example, the note on BM 35380 in Tablet XI records 'New joins: BM 36114 + BM 36225 (Jiménez)'). Humans still decide restorations and translate. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/XI ; https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091
ai_pipeline_stage: Fragment matching only, and upstream of the edition. The Fragmentarium's alignment search proposes new Gilgamesh pieces, and that is how the fragment of the latest datable manuscript was found. Building the score, restoring gaps and translating are all human work.
scale_metrics: The Standard Babylonian Tablets I to XII give 2,683 edited lines and 146 manuscript entries in the API. Tablet I has 17 manuscripts over 300 lines, Tablet XI 17 over 329 lines, Tablet XII 11 over 139 lines and Tablet IX only 3 over 137 lines. The 146 entries count joined fragments and excerpt or quotation tablets separately; the site's introduction puts the 'canonical' version at 'some 75 manuscripts' [uncertain]. Manuscripts come from Nineveh, Babylon, Assur, Uruk and Kalhu and run from 8th-century BC Assyria to 2nd-century BC Babylonia. Across all 39 chapters the edition gives about 3,150 verses. It sits on a Fragmentarium of about 25,000 tablets and 350,000+ lines (2024), published under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4 ; https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/I ; https://openhumanitiesdata.metajnl.com/articles/10.5334/johd.148
what_was_found: The edition is the container for the finds rather than a single find. It holds George's 2003 text plus everything since: the Sulaymaniyah Tablet V lines on the Cedar Forest (2014), the Ugarit and 'civilizing of Ea-Enkidu' tablets George published in 2007, Jiménez's 2020 fragments from the British Museum's Babylon collection (source of the new XI 74 reading), later Fragmentarium joins, and uncertain fragments flagged but not yet placed (Sm 1754 and K 16024 in Tablet I). It sets the Old and Middle Babylonian tablets beside the Standard version as separate chapters instead of merging them. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4 ; https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/I
provenance_and_ethics: The manuscripts are registered museum holdings: mostly the British Museum (Kuyunjik and Babylon collections), plus the Vorderasiatisches Museum Berlin (the Assur tablets, VAT numbers), the Iraq Museum (IM numbers) and the Schøyen Collection for some Old Babylonian pieces. Schøyen material is the ethically awkward part, since the collection has faced repeated questions about how Iraqi antiquities left the country after 1991; the edition includes Schøyen Gilgamesh tablets without comment on their route [uncertain]. The clay stays in London, Berlin and Baghdad. The digital text lives in Munich, open to read, with data under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and code under the MIT licence on GitHub. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4 ; https://openhumanitiesdata.metajnl.com/articles/10.5334/johd.148 ; https://github.com/ElectronicBabylonianLiterature
ai_craft_tension: The eBL edition sharpens the contrast between a book and a database. George's 2003 edition is a fixed object: two volumes, one reading per line, one date on the spine. The eBL version keeps changing. Every reading carries its manuscripts beneath it, every gap stays visible in brackets, and a new fragment turned up by the matching algorithm can change a line next month. Machines do the plumbing well here. They align each tablet's signs to the reconstruction, cross-link the parallel passages and surface candidate fragments. They do not choose between restorations. At XI 74 the editors print 'I lavished', then give half a dozen alternatives in a note, including one from George himself and one from Eckart Frahm, and call the problem 'not easy'. A human judgement settles the line. It can be undone, and it is honestly labelled as provisional. A poet translating from this edition has more evidence than any before, and more uncertainty to face. The score shows how little any single tablet holds. Turning that into a line of English still takes someone who can hear the poem.
essay_hooks: (1) A printed edition versus a living one: George's 2003 text is fixed on the page, while the eBL edition says it 'incorporates all discoveries since then, both large and small' (eBL introduction to L I.4). (2) Tablet XI line 74: 'I lavished on my workforce like the waters of a river', printed with a note listing rival readings from George and Frahm and calling them 'not easy' (eBL SB XI 74). (3) Tablet IX, where Gilgamesh grieves for Enkidu, survives on only 3 manuscripts; Tablet I survives on 17 (eBL API). (4) Manuscripts span about 600 years of copying, from 8th-century BC Assyria to 2nd-century BC Babylonia. (5) The poem's last lines repeat the opening description of Uruk's walls, and the edition links XI 323 to 328 directly back to I 18 to 23. (6) Arabic beside English for Tablets I to III, translated at the University of Baghdad. (7) The text is a DOI and a JSON endpoint as well as a book, openly licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Sources: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4 ; https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/XI ; https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/SB/I ; https://openhumanitiesdata.metajnl.com/articles/10.5334/johd.148
